# Running IDEBench on ClickHouse

This directory contains everything needed to run IDEBench against [ClickHouse](https://clickhouse.com/).
Two drivers are provided in `drivers/`:

* `clickhouse`: exact, blocking execution of the SQL generated by IDEBench. A query that exceeds the
  time requirement is cancelled by the server (`max_execution_time`) and reported as a violation without a result.
* `clickhouse_online`: approximate execution. At the start of each workflow the driver measures the scan
  throughput, and every query then reads at most as many rows as fit into half of the time requirement
  (`max_rows_to_read` with `read_overflow_mode = 'break'`). The aggregate over the rows read is returned,
  with `COUNT` results scaled by `total_rows / read_rows`; `AVG` needs no scaling. The estimate is valid because
  the rows produced by `datagen.py` are i.i.d., so the rows read first are a uniform sample.
  The time requirement is enforced in the same way as for the exact driver.

Both drivers use the HTTP interface of ClickHouse and only the Python standard library.
The server URL can be passed as the only element of `driver-args`; otherwise it is taken from the `CLICKHOUSE_URL`
environment variable, with the default `http://localhost:8123/`.
The dataset size selects the database: a run with `"settings-sizes": ["500m"]` queries `idebench_500m.tbl_flights`.

## 1. Generate the data

Unzip `data/flights.zip` as described in the wiki, then generate the data with `datagen.py`, e.g. 500K rows:

```
python datagen.py --sample-file data/flights/sample.csv --sample-descriptor data/flights/sample.json --size 500000
```

`datagen.py` is single-threaded and needs about 0.5 s per 100K rows, i.e. hours for 1B rows.
`clickhouse/gen_parallel.py` runs the same generator code in parallel and writes files of 10M rows each
(`part_000.csv` ... ). Batch `i` is always seeded with `seed + i`, so the output is identical to a serial run,
and the first N files form exactly the dataset of N * 10M rows. For example, 1B rows with 24 processes
(each process needs a few GB of memory):

```
mkdir gen
python clickhouse/gen_parallel.py . gen 100 24
```

## 2. Load the data

Start a ClickHouse server (see https://clickhouse.com/docs/getting-started/quick-start) and load the files
into the database `idebench_<size>`. A header line, as written by `datagen.py`, is detected automatically.

```
clickhouse/load.sh 500k dataset.csv
clickhouse/load.sh 100m gen/part_00{0..9}.csv
clickhouse/load.sh 1b gen/part_*.csv
```

Set `CH` to change the client command, e.g. `CH="clickhouse client --host myhost" clickhouse/load.sh ...`.
The table definition is in `clickhouse/schema.sql`. It uses plain types and no sorting key, so that no
tuning is applied for the workload.

## 3. Compute the ground truth

The exact driver without a time limit produces the ground truth for all workflows in `data/flights/workflows/`:

```
cp data/flights/default_workflows/*.json data/flights/workflows/
python idebench.py --settings-dataset flights --settings-size 500k --driver-name clickhouse --settings-thinktime 0 --groundtruth
```

## 4. Run the benchmark

`clickhouse/runconfig.json` runs the ten mixed workflows with both drivers for all time requirements used in
the paper, on the dataset of 500K rows:

```
python idebench.py --run-config clickhouse/runconfig.json
```

The detailed reports are written to `reports/`. `clickhouse/summarize.py` prints a summary table with the mean
percentage of violated time requirements, the mean percentage of missing bins and statistics of the mean relative
error over the queries that did not violate the time requirement:

```
python clickhouse/summarize.py reports
python clickhouse/summarize.py reports interface,size,wtype,time_requirement
```

Note that timings are sensitive to other load on the machine; use a dedicated machine for meaningful results.
